1.note: 'of course' is a parenthetical needing both commas; B and D drop one, C's semicolon leaves 'of course, but in Britain...' as a non-clause.

2.note: Idiom is 'spend on'; 'invest on', 'devote on', 'pay on' are all unidiomatic. The sentence in the stem decides it.

3.note: The next sentence (readers stop buying, authors earn nothing) makes the publishers' view 'reckless'. The stem sentence alone would allow any of them.

4.note: Absolute phrase 'their covers divided into...'. Risk: B and C are wrong only if 'divided' is read as a participle; a student reading it as an intransitive past verb ('covers divided into bands') could defend B or C. Because both would then be equally right, neither is uniquely defensible.

5.note: Comma splice fixed by ', but'; '; and' and ', however,' are both errors.

6.note: The previous sentence, 'Lane did not wait for bookshops', sets up 'Instead'. Needs that sentence, which the stem does not include.

7.note: Plural subject 'Sales' needs 'were'; past tense matches 'sold'. B is wrong in tense and in number.

8.note: The addition breaks the sales focus. D is false (paragraph 1 does not say that), and C is tempting but the sentence interrupts 'paid off' -> sales.

9.note: DEFECT: C fixes the dangling modifier but makes 'paperbacks were carried by soldiers ... and passed them along', where 'paperbacks' ends up as the subject of 'passed them'. D has the same flaw. No option yields a fully grammatical sentence.

10.note: The phrase is a familiar price comparison. Guessable from the stem's quoted phrase alone; A and D are obviously off, and B is false (the objection was about lost hardback sales).

11.note: 'mimic' is the precise word for imitating texture; mock, parody and rehearse are wrong or carry ridicule.

12.note: A paired dash sets off the color list; the other options mismatch the dash or use a double colon.

13.note: 'they' agrees with 'the muscles'; 'it' and 'this' leave the antecedent mismatched or vague.

14.note: 'each ... is'. The present tense matches 'can open'.

15.note: Inverted sentence whose subject is 'two other layers', so it needs 'lie'. 'lays' is the wrong verb.

16.note: Taste is irrelevant to color detection. C is false (paragraph 3 says nothing about arms), and B is tempting but off-axis. The stem's quoted pupil/hue sentence lets you choose D without the passage. Stem wording 'at the end of ... third sentence' is odd and should read 'after'.

17.note: Nonrestrictive 'which' needs the comma because 'only one type' already identifies the pigment. B could be defended by a student who reads it as a restrictive 'which', but the standard ACT rule favors A.

18.note: Contrast with 'appears to be colorblind' in the previous sentence calls for 'Even so'; the other three options are causal or additive.

19.note: Paragraphs 2-3 describe the mechanism. D is false (the eyes are colorblind). A's wording mirrors the purpose statement, so it can be chosen without the passage.

20.note: Comma splice fixed by a semicolon. C's 'although' is illogical (it should be causal), and B's ', yet,' is still a splice.

21.note: Appositive takes a comma; C puts 'that' in a nonrestrictive clause, and D's semicolon leaves a fragment.

22.note: The narrator is unimpressed, so the plain 'did only one thing' fits. TELL: three grandiose options (feat/wonder/triumph) against one plain one, so the odd-one-out is the key without the passage.

23.note: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; B is a splice, D is fused, C's comma after 'and' is wrong.

24.note: Sets up 'for forty seconds at a time' (and the title). C is a false causal claim. D quotes the echo of the stem sentence, so it is guessable without the passage.

25.note: Past-tense narration ('would take', 'cut keys badly'). Present 'scolds' is grammatical in isolation, so the context sentence is needed.

26.note: 'never scolds ... Instead, he would' is a contrast with the negated action; Therefore, Moreover and Also do not fit.

27.note: Possessive 'whose husband'; whom, who and who's all fail.

28.note: Paragraphs 4-5 show the narrator learning what keys meant to customers. D paraphrases the purpose ('people it served' -> 'customers'), so it is guessable without the passage. A and C are partial and too narrow.

29.note: Missing main verb, so 'is'. B and D leave a fragment.

30.note: 'sign' is neutral and fits beginning, ending and harder to manage alike. 'symptom' is negative and wrong for 'beginning', 'omen' is supernatural, 'signal flare' is literal.

31.note: A colon introduces an explanation after an independent clause; B and D leave a fragment, C is fused.

32.note: Efforts (fences, signs) followed by failure is a contrast, so 'However'. Needs the preceding sentence.

33.note: 'no better' needs the fence/hedge failure sentence before it, so Point D, after [C]'s sentence. Points A-C come before any failure has been described.

34.note: 'Rather than deciding in advance...' is the reverse of fighting the paths, so 'opposite'. 'customary' contradicts 'some'.

35.note: Fused sentence fixed by ', and'; B's '; and,' and D's splice are both wrong.

36.note: Plural 'officials' needs 'have studied'; C and D are singular.

37.note: The parenthetical 'for instance' needs both commas.

39.note: Figurative 'read' (interpret). 'carefully' rules out skim and browse; 'proofread' is too literal. The antecedent of 'them' (desire paths) is three sentences back, which is slightly loose.

40.note: The essay presents waiting to pave as one practice and grants that barriers are sometimes right (paragraph 5). A is a true detail but does not make the argument, and C is false.
